title: What helps pelvic girdle pain during pregnancy?
seoTitle: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy: what helps
description: PGP can make stairs, rolling in bed or getting out of a car painful. See NHS and RCOG coping steps, physiotherapy options and when to seek care.
primaryQuestion: How can I relieve pelvic pain during pregnancy?
directAnswer: Pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain (PGP)—sometimes still called SPD—is discomfort around the pelvic joints that can make walking, stairs, dressing or rolling in bed harder. UK NHS and RCOG patient information say it is common, is not harmful to the baby, and often eases with early assessment, activity pacing, practical task changes and physiotherapy. Not every ache in the pelvis is PGP: bleeding, fever, urinary pain or sudden severe symptoms need maternity or emergency care first.

sections.heading: What PGP and SPD describe
paragraphs: The NHS explains that some women develop pelvic pain in pregnancy, sometimes called pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain (PGP) or symphysis pubis dysfunction (SPD). PGP is a group of uncomfortable symptoms linked to stiffness of the pelvic joints or the joints moving unevenly at the front or back of the pelvis.

RCOG patient information describes PGP as pain in the front and/or back of the pelvis that can also affect the hips or thighs, and notes that PGP used to be known as SPD. Both sources estimate it affects about 1 in 5 pregnant women to some degree. The NHS states PGP is not harmful to your baby, though it can be painful and limit how easily you move.

Pain may sit over the pubic bone, across one or both sides of the lower back, in the perineum, or spread into the thighs. Some people notice clicking or grinding. Our guide to pregnancy backache covers low-back patterns that can overlap; location alone is not a self-diagnosis.

sections.heading: Daily tasks worth describing at assessment
paragraphs: NHS guidance lists common aggravators: walking, stairs, standing on one leg (for example when dressing), turning over in bed, and moving the legs apart (such as getting out of a car). RCOG adds long walks on uneven ground and pain during sexual intercourse as possible triggers.

Write down which of those tasks are hardest, how far you can walk before pain rises, and whether one side feels more unstable. That detail helps a physiotherapist match advice to real life rather than guessing from a generic stretch list.

UK NHS advice is to call your midwife or GP if pelvic pain makes it hard to move around, hurts when you get out of a car or turn in bed, or makes stairs painful—these can be signs of pregnancy-related PGP that deserve assessment rather than waiting until birth.

sections.heading: Practical easing steps and physiotherapy options
paragraphs: NHS coping advice includes keeping active while avoiding tasks that clearly worsen pain, resting when you can, wearing supportive shoes, putting equal weight on each leg when standing, sitting to dress, using a pillow between the legs in bed, and keeping the knees together when getting in and out of a car. Avoid long standing or sitting, climbing stairs more than needed, and lifting heavy shopping.

RCOG adds changing position often (try not to sit more than about 30 minutes at a time), lying on the less painful side, and avoiding stooping or twisting to carry a toddler on one hip. Treat these as trials: keep what helps for a few days and drop what flares symptoms.

You may be referred to physiotherapy for obstetric pelvic joint problems. NHS guidance says physiotherapy aims to ease pain, improve muscle function and improve pelvic joint position and stability, and may include exercises for the pelvic floor, stomach, back and hips, plus crutches or a pelvic support belt when needed. Dr. Zalak Shah (PT) can build a task-based plan once maternity care has ruled out urgent medical causes; she does not replace obstetric assessment.

sections.heading: How support needs can shift as pregnancy advances
paragraphs: RCOG notes that PGP is more common later in pregnancy as the bump grows and load on the pelvis increases. A belt, shorter standing bouts or help with shopping that felt optional mid-pregnancy may become useful later—and may be needed less after birth, when symptoms often improve.

Around 1 in 10 women have ongoing pain after birth according to RCOG; continued physiotherapy and GP follow-up matter if symptoms persist. Mention PGP in your birth plan so labour supporters know to keep your legs supported and help with position changes. Most women with PGP can still have a vaginal birth; RCOG states a caesarean is not normally required for PGP alone.

sections.heading: When pelvic pain needs urgent maternity review
paragraphs: Seek same-day maternity advice if pelvic or lower abdominal pain comes with vaginal bleeding, fever, pain when you pee, a suspected waters break, rhythmic painful tightenings, or a clear drop in baby movements once movements are established. Sudden collapse, chest pain or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency services (in India, dial 112).

If movement is severely limited, RCOG notes a higher clot risk and advises discussing stockings or other medical prevention with your maternity team—do not self-start medicines. After urgent problems are excluded, return to pacing and prenatal physiotherapy rather than pushing through sharp pelvic instability.

faqs.question: Is pelvic girdle pain the same as ordinary pregnancy backache?
faqs.answer: Not always. PGP centres on the pelvic joints and often flares with stairs, single-leg standing or parting the legs. Backache can overlap. Our pregnancy back-pain guide covers low-back comfort tips; a clinician sorts which pattern fits your symptoms.

faqs.question: Will PGP harm the baby?
faqs.answer: NHS and RCOG patient information both say PGP is not harmful to the baby. The main impact is on your comfort and mobility, which is why earlier assessment and physiotherapy are encouraged.
